structure.title: 3. Why Does the BB Portfolio Outperform?
4. A Text-Based Measure of Brand Value

observations.statement: The estimand is the abnormal return (alpha) of a long-only portfolio of top brands, estimated as the intercept of time-series factor regressions across several named factor models, and as the average slope on a top-brand indicator in Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions.

The introduction walks through alternative explanations (riskier intangible investment, organization capital, an omitted mispriced variable) and argues why each is unlikely, then explicitly concedes there is no natural experiment and results are open to noncausal interpretation, citing peer papers with the same limitation.
observations.quote: we do not have a natural experiment that exogenously assigns different brand values to firms

observations.statement: Portfolio formation is timed to the first day of the month after the list announcement so that the short-term announcement reaction is excluded; the authors state the delay lets the market price the news before the return window starts.
observations.locator: Section 1.1 end; Section 2 opening and footnote 10

observations.statement: The main signal is a commercial annual best-brands list; brands are mapped to stocks, analysis is at the stock level, and only U.S. companies with CRSP price data are kept, so private companies drop out. The sample period runs from the first list year to the end of the CRSP sample used.
The data section documents the vendor's list eligibility criteria and its three-step valuation methodology at length, and justifies the source by its long time series covering booms and crises.

For the cross-sectional regressions the universe is CRSP ordinary common shares on the three main exchanges, with a minimum number of monthly returns per year, matched to Compustat with a standard six-month lag of accounting data justified by filing timing in a footnote.

Each regression table reports the number of observations (months for factor regressions, stock-months for Fama-MacBeth); the text flags that adding advertising and brand-capital controls shrinks the sample because missing items are dropped, following the literature's practice.

For the text-based measure the authors download all annual filings from SEC EDGAR since digital filing became mandatory, drop duplicates and amendments, merge with CRSP/Compustat, keep December fiscal year-ends, and impose a market-cap floor to keep small caps out of the portfolio.
The input-measure analysis starts the CRSP/Compustat sample in the first year with adequate advertising disclosure and reports results both for the vendor-list period and the full available period.
The treatment is a dummy equal to one if the stock is in the most recent best-brands list; a later analysis swaps the dummy for the log of the vendor's estimated brand value to test intensity.

Each characteristic control (beta, log size, book-to-market, momentum, asset growth, profitability, illiquidity, R&D, idiosyncratic volatility, skewness, advertising, brand and organization capital) is defined in the text and again in the table notes with its estimation window; all independent variables are winsorized at the 1st and 99th percentiles.

Brand capital and organization capital stocks are built by the perpetual inventory method, with parameters and sample selection explicitly borrowed from named prior papers; the input-measure section states the depreciation rate and initial-stock growth assumption used.

The novel text measure counts occurrences of brand(s) in each annual filing normalized by total words after stop-word removal; top-N portfolios are formed on this ratio. The authors describe it as parsimonious and note that noise in the measure works against finding results.

Earnings surprises are actual EPS minus the median analyst forecast scaled by price at one- and two-year horizons, and actual long-run EPS growth minus the long-term growth forecast; large forecast errors are trimmed following prior literature, and forecast timing relative to fiscal year-end is justified in a footnote.
Announcement returns are cumulative abnormal returns defined as compounded stock return minus the value-weighted market return over a three-day window around the earnings announcement date.

To separate internally versus externally built brands, the best-brand dummy is split into two dummies by a yearly median split of balance-sheet intangibles over total assets; a footnote reports the auxiliary regression supporting the assumed negative correlation between acquired and internal intangibles.

The main factor table has one column per factor model, reports alpha and every factor loading with t-statistics in parentheses, the number of months, and a note listing the factors in each model, the standard error method, the sample period and the star thresholds.

The Fama-MacBeth table adds controls progressively across five columns, labels the second column as the full model, and reports the total observations and average R-squared; the notes restate every variable definition.

The announcement-return table lists year and industry fixed effects as Yes/No rows and adds controls across columns; the earnings-surprise table states in notes that all regressions include year and industry fixed effects and that coefficients are rescaled.

The weighting table stacks the original equal-weighted alphas with alphas after excluding small caps, straight value weighting, and capped value weighting at two NYSE percentiles, keeping the same five model columns for comparison.

Later tables report only the coefficient of interest (alpha or the brand dummy) plus rows of Yes/No indicators for controls, advertising, brand/org capital, nonmissing requirement and industry adjustment, rather than full coefficient lists.

Newey-West standard errors are used for factor regressions with the stated reason of allowing heteroskedastic and serially correlated residuals; the same method is stated in the notes of the Fama-MacBeth tables without a separate justification or lag length.
observations.quote: to allow for residuals to be heteroscedastic and serially correlated

observations.statement: For the earnings-surprise and announcement-return panel regressions the tables give t-statistics but the text and notes do not state the standard error type or any clustering level.
Results are reported across five factor models and many specifications and described as robust when significant in all; no multiple-testing adjustment is mentioned.

Before the return tests the paper documents the size distribution of the portfolio firms against NYSE breakpoints (table and figure) to pre-empt the micro-cap concern for equal weighting, and uses that to motivate the choice of equal-weighted portfolios as the headline.
List turnover (additions and drops per year) and industry composition over time are tabulated and plotted to characterize the signal's persistence before returns are analyzed.
The text-based measure is validated informally by listing well-known brands that rank at the top, by industry breadth, and by reporting its correlation with the vendor-based portfolio.
A footnote reports checking the announcement-day return of list inclusion to rule out a discount-rate shock story, citing an external study with the same direction.

Factor-model robustness uses alternative benchmarks (industry- and characteristics-adjusted returns, reported in the Internet Appendix), alternative profitability and liquidity factors in a footnote, and replacement or augmentation of the value factor with three intangible-adjusted HML factors plus fully intangible-adjusted factors in a main-text table.

Fama-MacBeth robustness covers industry-adjusted dependent variables, keeping observations with missing advertising by zero-filling plus a missing indicator, and a continuous brand-value regressor; these are relegated to the Internet Appendix or footnotes with a one-paragraph summary.

Subperiod robustness is done by re-estimating excess returns within named macro regimes and within five-year blocks, comparing mean with median monthly excess returns, and plotting cumulative alpha-plus-residuals for each model.

Several checks are described only in prose as unreported or not tabulated for brevity (organization-capital factor, an input-based brand factor, brand importance sorts, alternative top-N cutoffs, value-weighted input portfolios), some with point estimates given in footnotes.

Overlap with a rival list-based anomaly (best workplaces) is handled by adding that portfolio's return as an extra factor and its indicator as an extra regressor, shown side by side with the original columns.

The only heterogeneity cut is the high versus low reported-intangibles split of best brands, which is explicitly motivated by the accounting-treatment mechanism and reported for raw and industry-adjusted returns across four specifications.

Mechanisms are addressed in a dedicated section with five sub-tests: value of rebalancing, exposure to intangible factors, overlap with another list anomaly, internal versus acquired intangibles, and analyst earnings surprises plus announcement returns.

The rebalancing test compares a never-rebalanced portfolio from an early list with the annually rebalanced portfolio across all five models, with the prediction stated before the result; the choice of base year is justified in a footnote.

Monthly alphas are translated into annual and cumulative excess returns over the sample; the announcement-return effect is scaled by four announcements a year to express the share of alpha it accounts for, and described as a conservative lower bound because of post-announcement drift.
The number of firms per year is benchmarked against prior list-based anomaly studies, and the input-versus-output contrast is compared to an R&D efficiency paper.
The authors acknowledge the absence of exogenous variation, concede that an omitted mispriced variable cannot be excluded outright, and note that the text measure is deliberately crude.

The text-based portfolio is framed as an out-of-sample test because it extends to years before the vendor list exists and to many more firms; the U.S.-only and single-vendor scope is stated but not discussed further.

Tables use three-level significance stars with t-statistics in parentheses; notes restate the sample period, the standard error method, and the factor composition of every model in each table, repeated verbatim across tables.

Figures include an industry count bar chart, a heat map of industry affiliation by year, a size-category share plot, a cumulative excess-return line plot by model, and a bar-style comparison of alphas across models; a two-year summary statistics table gives first and last sample years.
Supplementary results are referenced as Internet Appendix Table or Figure numbers; the appendix is hosted by the publisher and is not part of the text read here.

The introduction opens with practitioner epigraphs, motivates limitations of the input measure, previews the main results and mechanisms, positions against the closest paper, and has a contribution paragraph; a long data and descriptive section precedes the methodology section.

Empirical sections proceed from the headline factor regressions, to weighting sensitivity, to characteristic-controlled regressions, to time-series stability, then a separate mechanisms section, then the alternative measure and the input measure as a contrast; no roadmap paragraph is given.
Each subsection closes with an Overall sentence summarizing what the tests show, and each mechanism subsection states the hypothesis and expected sign before presenting the table.
A code availability statement at the end of the conclusion gives a Harvard Dataverse DOI for the replication code; no data availability statement or software name is given in the text.

Inputs are commercial databases (CRSP, Compustat, IBES), a commercial vendor's public brand list, factor data from named authors' websites and one set of factors obtained directly from other authors (acknowledged in a footnote), and filings scraped from SEC EDGAR.

gaps: No standard error type or clustering justification is given for the earnings-surprise and announcement-return regressions.
Newey-West lag length is never stated in the text.
No data availability statement and no software named; only a code DOI.
No explicit roadmap paragraph in the introduction.
No formal validation test of the text-based measure beyond example firms and a correlation with the vendor portfolio.
Several robustness checks are described as unreported or not tabulated.

reading.note: All 43 pages read in five chunks; pages 39 to 43 are references and were skimmed. The Internet Appendix is hosted by the publisher and was not part of the text file.
